data.description:
## Problem

The `bedrock-spend-cap` Lambda prices Bedrock usage from a rate card held in SSM `/bedrock-spend-cap/state` under `rates`. That card contains no entry for any Anthropic Claude model. Every invocation logs a fail-closed fallback for the model family that rebar's own LLM operations actually run on:

```
[WARNING] no rate for model=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 metric=InputTokenCount; using fail-closed fallback
[WARNING] no rate for model=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 metric=CacheWriteInputTokenCount; using fail-closed fallback
[WARNING] no rate for model=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 metric=OutputTokenCount; using fail-closed fallback
[WARNING] no rate for model=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0 metric=CacheReadInputTokenCount; using fail-closed fallback
```

These four lines repeat on every scheduled run. The rate card does carry entries for DeepSeek, Llama 3.3, Nova (Lite/Micro/Pro/2.0 Lite), Pixtral, Titan embeddings, gpt-oss, Mistral Large 3, and MiniMax — that is, for models the project does not primarily use, while the primary family is unpriced.

## Why this matters

The Lambda drives two control actions. The lower threshold emits a warning that project guidance now uses to pause all agent work until the next day. The upper threshold attaches a deny policy to every target role, which takes down the review bot and every rebar gate at once. Both actions are therefore triggered by a number that, for the dominant workload, is a synthetic fallback rather than a measured rate.

The direction of the error is unknown and matters in both directions:

- If the fallback over-prices, the project pauses work it did not need to pause and eventually denies Bedrock access while genuinely under budget. The cost is lost delivery time and a self-inflicted outage.
- If the fallback under-prices, real overspend runs past both thresholds without either firing. The cost is an unbounded bill and a control that reports healthy while failing.

Neither can currently be ruled out, because the fallback rate's relationship to actual Claude pricing is not established anywhere in the parameter or the logs.

This is the same class of defect as `enviable-beloved-buffalo` (a metric that cannot change state carries no information) and `catty-giddied-hedgehog` (an alarm latched for days without anyone owning it). A control whose input is not trustworthy is not a control, whichever way it errs.

## Investigation notes

`rates_day` is `2026-09-17`, so the card is being refreshed — the omission is not staleness. This points at the rate-loading path filtering out or failing to resolve the Anthropic entries, rather than at an out-of-date snapshot. That is a hypothesis and needs confirming against the loader before any fix.

Note also that the fallback is silent in effect: it emits a `WARNING` to the Lambda log, but the resulting spend figure is published to SSM with no marker distinguishing a measured value from a partly-synthetic one. A consumer reading the parameter cannot tell that the number is estimated.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The root cause is confirmed by observation: identify why the rate loader yields no Anthropic entries while populating other providers, rather than assuming staleness or an upstream omission.
- [ ] The fallback rate's actual relationship to real Claude pricing is established and recorded, so the historical direction and rough magnitude of the error is known rather than guessed.
- [ ] A failing test reproduces the condition before any fix: a rate card lacking the primary model family must be detectable rather than silently tolerated.
- [ ] Anthropic Claude models used by rebar's LLM operations are priced from real rates.
- [ ] An unpriced model in the workload is surfaced as an actionable signal, not only as a log line — a spend figure computed with any fallback component is marked as estimated where it is published, so consumers can tell a measured value from a synthetic one.
- [ ] Threshold behaviour is re-validated after the fix, so the warning and deny actions are known to fire against real spend.
data.title: Bedrock spend cap cannot price the primary model family and falls back silently, so both thresholds fire on a synthetic number
